RagShortTexts: Sarmatian covers distinct groups; it is not a single uniform fourth-century state.
Herds, grazing and dependants' safety constrain a mounted following's choices.

Variants.Content: Sarmatian is a broad designation covering groups with different locations and relationships, not a single uniform state. In the module, authority can depend on kin connections, herds, access to grazing and a leader's armed following. Relations with Rome or other steppe peoples may offer protection and opportunity while exposing dependants to new obligations. The pressure of movements farther east need not be identical at every camp in 374, and later Hunnic domination is not certain knowledge for every speaker. Disputes over movement, supplies and the protection of households distinguish this politics from invented senatorial courts and castle-based fiefs.

A mounted follower needs a sound horse, forage and a place where the household's animals can rest. An order to move quickly may conflict with the pace of children and loaded carts. Men argue over scouts and watering places because a mistake can cost the herd, even when no enemy has yet reached the camp.

A Sarmatian leader weighs an offer of outside protection against the men, supplies or obedience it may require. Other households may prefer a different route or patron. Prestige alone cannot settle grazing and security; a workable bargain must leave dependants able to live, rather than rescue only the chief's immediate companions.
